document_title: Weight, Cold, Mountains. The Army's Alaska Drone Taken Apart
post_copy:
"Soldiers across the 11th Airborne Division continue to demonstrate that many of the best ideas come from the bottom up."

Col. Matthew Adamczyk is right.

Weight. Sgt. 1st Class Devin McNamara enabled unarmed payload flights before the live strikes.
Cold. Pfc. Michael Pereira hand-sewed a body-heat battery vault.
Mountains. Spc. Leighton Keilen won Angel Ascent with a Skydio drone relay.
Snow. Capt. Daniel Woodard's team designed a metal hatch cover other units can copy for about $300 in materials.

Soldiers get names. The drone's model, payload mass, endurance, engagement range and measured accuracy don't.

Inside, the first kinetic drone strike within the Richardson Training Area, four soldier fixes and five drone specs left blank.

A $300 hatch got its price printed. Should an armed drone's measured accuracy be that public?

#11thAirborne #ArcticDrones #AlaskaDefense

slides.headline: Weight. Cold. Mountains. The Army's Alaska drone, taken apart.
The first kinetic drone strike in the Richardson Training Area.
slides.body: Paratroopers of the 2nd Mobile Brigade Combat Team (Airborne), 11th Airborne Division, flew armed first-person view drones in live fire, alongside sniper teams, reconnaissance elements and a gun truck.
labels: ARMY RECOGNITION SAYS NOT TO READ IT AS THE ARMY'S FIRST EXPLOSIVE FPV USE
ONE GROOVE PER LIVE-FIRE DAY, TRUE CALENDAR SPACING

slides.headline: Before the strike, they flew the weight.
slides.body: Operators first flew unarmed explosive payloads to see how the added weight changed the drone's maneuverability. Sgt. 1st Class Devin McNamara, the brigade's sUAS master trainer, helped enable the test flights.

slides.headline: What the Army left blank.
labels: NOT IDENTIFIED BY THE ARMY, ARMY RECOGNITION REPORTED ON OCTOBER 28TH

slides.headline: A private hand-sewed a battery vault.
slides.body: Pfc. Michael Pereira's passive prototype is designed to keep drone batteries viable in sub-zero temperatures using only body heat and radiant barriers. It was an entry at Angel Ascent, the 11th Airborne's innovation competition, on October 28th.
labels: STUDIO DRAWING FROM THE ARMY'S DESCRIPTION

slides.headline: First place went to a relay over the ridge.
slides.body: Spc. Leighton Keilen won Angel Ascent, and a Meritorious Service Medal, with a Skydio drone relay and modular payload delivery system. The Army says it significantly extends tactical drone range in Alaska's mountains.
labels: A CHUGACH PROFILE, DRAWN TO SHOW LINE OF SIGHT. NOT THE SITE.

slides.headline: Not every fix flies. About $300 in materials.
slides.body: It replaces cloth gunner hatch covers that let snow leak into truck cabs.
labels: "We put together a metal version that can sustain the weight of snow, and can also be popped open easily."
CAPT. DANIEL WOODARD, 725TH LIGHT SUPPORT BATTALION

Sources, primary first
U.S. Army (army.mil), by Correy Mathews, 2nd Mobile Brigade Combat Team (Airborne) live-fire exercises and the first kinetic drone strike within the Richardson Training Area, 2026-10-27, https://www.army.mil/article/296380
U.S. Army (army.mil), by Capt. Luke Smith, the 11th Airborne Division's Angel Ascent innovation competition and its winners, 2026-11-02, https://www.army.mil/article/296502
U.S. Army (army.mil), by Master Sgt. Adam Ross, preview of the second Angel Ascent and the 725th Light Support Battalion's metal hatch cover, 2026-10-21, https://www.army.mil/article/296265
Army Recognition, by Alain Servaes, US Army paratroopers integrate armed FPV drones in Alaska first live-fire exercises, 2026-10-28, https://www.armyrecognition.com/news/army-news/2026/us-army-paratroopers-integrate-armed-fpv-drones-in-alaska-first-live-fire-exercises

None of these four reports names AI or autonomy, so the deck covers these drones as Alaska defense robotics and claims nothing more. The quad, the battery vault and the hatch on the slides are studio drawings. The ridge is a real Chugach profile drawn to show line of sight, not the training site.

Every past deck, and the live docket of Alaska's open AI decisions, is at https://alaskaaihq.com
Served with the 11th Airborne or flown drones through an Alaska winter? Add context in the replies, with a public source where one exists.
aftercare: Post Thursday November 5th, or Tuesday November 10th to Thursday November 12th, 8 to 11 a.m. Alaska time. Drafts arrive daily and you decide when to post. Wednesday November 11th is Veterans Day, so decide whether a deck about an armed drone strike suits that day's feed.
Paste the sources comment within 60 seconds of posting and pin it, with every URL as plain text so LinkedIn keeps the links. The deck has no music or produced media, so there's no credits comment.

Reply to every comment in the first 90 minutes, with claims only and no first person. If asked 'is this AI?', answer that the Army's three articles and Army Recognition describe no AI or autonomy, that the strike drones are first-person view drones flown by operators, and that the deck covers them as robotics (C01, C05). If someone brings up Skydio's onboard autonomy, say the Army's article doesn't describe how Keilen's relay flies (C16).

If asked 'where is the range?', say the record doesn't map it. The Army names the Multi-Purpose Training Range in the Richardson Training Area and gives no location beyond that (C03). The slide 06 ridge is a drawing and not the site, and the range should never be placed on JBER or near Anchorage.

If asked which drone, how far or how accurate, point to slide 04, where none of it is published (C12). If someone calls it the Army's first armed FPV strike, point to slide 02. It was the first within the Richardson Training Area, and Army Recognition cautions against reading it as the Army's first (C04, C13).
After 48 hours, note saves and comments for the ledger.
editor_notes_for_email: Honesty guards hold across caption, slides and comment. 'First' is always scoped to the Richardson Training Area (C04), and the caution against reading it as the Army's first explosive FPV use is attributed to Army Recognition (C13). No string puts the training area on JBER or near Anchorage, a claim the fact-checker killed. No performance figure exists (C12), so payload, distance and temperature read NOT PUBLISHED or unscaled. Quotes are verbatim (C25, C31), Pereira's unit is never named, and the penetrators on 08 are named and never drawn. This is a robotics story on an AI page, and it says so, none of the three army.mil articles or Army Recognition mentions AI or autonomy, no frame implies either, and the first comment says so plainly. Expect a reply about Skydio's onboard autonomy; the Army's article doesn't describe how the relay flies. The slide art is studio drawing where marked, the generic quad (01, 03, 09), the vault (05), the ridge positions (06, a real Chugach DEM profile labelled NOT THE SITE) and the hatch shape (07). Five copywriter tightenings were applied to the render (the payload tag, the Army Recognition scope line, 'is designed to keep', the vault drawing note, the hatch headline), and the Fairbanks coordinate was removed from the Chugach section on 06.
